newsitem.title: EGYPT: Sudan rebels say they wiped out state army force.
newsitem.headline: Sudan rebels say they wiped out state army force.

text.p: The Sudanese opposition in Cairo reported another victory in their fight against the Khartoum government and said their soldiers wiped out a detachment of government troops in the east on Sunday.

"Our soldiers clashed with the government troops north of our garrison in Keili and they killed 150 of them," opposition spokesman Farouq Abu Eissa told Reuters. Keili is 100 km (60 miles) south of Damazin, the Blue Nile capital where Sudanese troops are massing for a counterattack on the rebels.
"We also captured nine trucks, three heavy machineguns and two military vehicles," Abu Eissa added.

In a faxed statement, veteran rebel commander John Garang said that the clash, which took place between 5 a.m. and 7 a.m. local time (0300 to 0500 GMT), was proof that "the rebels can stand up to the forces of the National Islamic Front in Sudan".
"We have totally destroyed the 'Torrential Flood' troops of the army," it added. Torrential Flood is an army codename.
There was no independent confirmation of the report.
The opposition says it has seized several towns and garrisons in the Blue Nile area but the government only admits to the loss of Kurmuk and Qeissan near the Ethiopian border.

The rebels say their goal is to advance on Damazin, site of a hydroelectricity plant which supplies Khartoum with most its power, to put pressure on the Sudanese government and bring about a popular uprising.

The rebels have been fighting the government in the east of the country for a week but Sudanese officials have said that they are nothing but agents of Ethiopian and Eritrean forces, who they say are doing most of the fighting.
Both states have denied the charges and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak has said that he is certain that no foreign troops have entered Sudan.
Egypt has also raised the morale of the Cairo-based opposition by saying that it would not intervene in the fighting, which it described as an internal affair.
Last week Mubarak met Sudanese Vice-President al-Zubeir Mohammad Saleh and he told a meeting of intellectuals on Saturday that Egypt would not offer support.

"How can I support them (the Sudanese government) when they are squabbling with the Sudanese people and there are Sudanese in opposition?" Mubarak said. "How can Egypt intervene and hit the Sudanese?"

Egypt has never wholeheartedly given its approval to the Sudanese opposition despite poor relations with Sudan's Islamist government. Egypt accuses Sudan of sheltering three gunmen charged with trying to kill Mubarak in 1995.
But the Cairo-based dissidents welcomed Egypt's stand and vowed to step up their offensive.

"Egypt's position makes us joyful and comfortable and is the truth which we the Sudanese people have been fighting for," Abu Eissa said. "We are grateful to Egypt and we will continue to stand in one bunker and fight against the regime," he added.
In Khartoum, the government Sudan al-Hadith newspaper said state troops had made "big advances" in the east and that army morale was high.
"The mujahideen (holy fighters) have reaffirmed their keenness to liberate every inch from the hands of the Tigrean (Ethiopian) forces," the paper quoted an official as saying.
